Fain
FAYN
adv. or adj.
Old English fægen, “glad, joyful, eager.” In KJV usage chiefly adverbial: gladly, willingly, eagerly. The word survives only in stylized literary usage in modern English.

📖 Biblical Definition

Fain in the KJV means gladly, willingly, eagerly—an Old English adverb expressing the disposition of the soul that would gladly do or have a thing, often paired with an unfulfilled wish or unattained desire. The word’s most famous biblical use is the prodigal son: and he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him (Luke 15:16). The young man, having wasted his substance with riotous living and now reduced to feeding swine in a far country, would gladly have eaten the very husks the pigs ate—the deepest indignity in his desperate hunger—and no man gave unto him. The verb would fain carries the picture of yearning desire that cannot be satisfied: the disposition is there, the will is there, the hunger is acute, but the satisfaction is withheld. Other notable KJV uses include Acts 26:28: then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian. And Paul’s response (v. 29): I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds. Acts 28:27, Paul’s quotation of Isaiah 6 in interpretation of Israel’s hardening: lest they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them. Job 27:22: for God shall cast upon him, and not spare: he would fain flee out of his hand. The verb’s pastoral usefulness is its capture of the soul’s registered desire—particularly in the contexts of unsatisfied longing (the prodigal’s hunger), of ardent wish for another’s good (Paul’s wish for Agrippa), of the unbeliever’s vain flight from God’s judgment (Job 27), and of the soul’s reach after what is desired but unattained. Fain is the older English’s precise way of saying gladly-but-not-attained, willingly-but-not-realized, eagerly-but-withheld; and the prodigal’s would-fain-have-eaten-the-husks remains one of the most poignant single phrases in Scripture, naming the depth of his fall in the dignity of the older idiom.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FAIN as gladly; with joy or pleasure; with preference; usually with would, as in he would fain go; in scripture, the older English adverb capturing the disposition of glad-but-unattained desire (most famously the prodigal’s would-fain-have-eaten-the-husks).

expand to see more

FAIN, adv. — Gladly; with joy or pleasure; with preference. Usually employed with the auxiliary would; as, he would fain go.

FAIN, a. — Glad; pleased; rejoiced. (Archaic adjectival use.)

📖 Key Scripture

Luke 15:16 — "And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him."

Acts 26:28-29 — "Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian. And Paul said, I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds."

Job 27:22 — "For God shall cast upon him, and not spare: he would fain flee out of his hand."

Luke 13:31 — "The same day there came certain of the Pharisees, saying unto him, Get thee out, and depart hence: for Herod will fain kill thee."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Fain is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by being functionally lost from modern English; the loss in modern translations is small in vocabulary but real in cadence, especially in the prodigal’s would-fain-have-eaten-the-husks, where the older idiom carries the depth of his fall in a register the modern equivalents flatten.

expand to see more

Fain has dropped from modern English usage almost entirely. Modern translations of Luke 15:16 read he longed to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs were eating or he would have eagerly filled his belly with the carob pods; the rhetorical effect is different. Would fain have filled his belly with the husks carries an antique register of dignified pathos that the modernizations have not retained. The prodigal’s fall is portrayed with the gravity the older idiom supplies: a young man, who had wasted his father’s substance with riotous living, now reduced to a longing that would have been content with what the pigs ate, and even that was not granted. The reader who knows would fain hears the verse in its full pathos; the reader who hears only the modern equivalents hears a flatter version of the same incident.

This is, as with the other KJV archaisms covered in this batch, a small specimen of the larger pattern. The older vocabulary carries registers of pathos, dignity, and cadence the modern English equivalents have, in many places, lost. The case for the older language is not the rejection of the newer but the recognition that the KJV is doing work the modernizations sometimes cannot replicate—and the saint who reads the KJV in its own idiom recovers access to a register of Scripture that has shaped English Christian piety for four centuries and that is not entirely available in the modernizations. Would fain is one of the smaller and more poignant of these registers, and the prodigal’s use of it remains one of the most affecting single phrases in the English Bible.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English fægen (glad, eager); used in the KJV chiefly with would to express glad-but-unattained desire, most famously in the prodigal’s would-fain-have-eaten-the-husks (Luke 15:16).

expand to see more

Old English fægen — glad, eager (the etymological root).

Greek epithumeō (G1937) — to desire, long for (Luke 15:16, behind would fain).

Greek thelō (G2309) — to will, desire (Luke 13:31, behind will fain).

Hebrew chāphets (H2654) — to delight in, desire (the OT cousin verb of glad desire).

Usage

"He would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him—the prodigal’s fall named in the dignity of the older idiom."

"Would fain captures glad-but-unattained desire: the disposition is there, the satisfaction is withheld; the older adverb names what modern English equivalents flatten."

"Modern translations replace fain with longed, eagerly, or rephrase the construction; the older word carries antique cadence and pathos the substitutes have lost."
